hints: Focus on how oxidising power of the halogens and reducing power of the halides change as you go down Group 17.
Remember the order is $\text{F}_2 > \text{Cl}_2 > \text{Br}_2 > \text{I}_2$ for oxidising strength, and the reverse $\text{I}^- > \text{Br}^- > \text{Cl}^- > \text{F}^-$ for reducing strength.
A halide ion can only reduce a halogen above it in the group, while a halogen can only oxidise a halide ion below it, so check where $\text{Br}^-$ sits relative to $\text{Cl}_2$ and $\text{I}_2$.
walkthrough:
**Recall the Group 17 redox trends**

Think of it as a competition for electrons. Top halogens grab electrons best, bottom halide ions give electrons best.

Oxidising power: $$\text{F}_2 > \text{Cl}_2 > \text{Br}_2 > \text{I}_2$$
Reducing power: $$\text{I}^- > \text{Br}^- > \text{Cl}^- > \text{F}^-$$

**Apply the displacement rule**

A more powerful oxidiser displaces a less powerful one. So $\text{Cl}_2$ oxidises both $\text{Br}^-$ and $\text{I}^-$, but $\text{Br}_2$ only oxidises $\text{I}^-$.

Example reaction that does happen:
$$\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{Br}^- \rightarrow 2\text{Cl}^- + \text{Br}_2$$

**Test Br- as a reducing agent**

$\text{Br}^-$ is a stronger reducing agent than $\text{Cl}^-$, so it can give electrons to $\text{Cl}_2$ and reduce it to $\text{Cl}^-$. But $\text{Br}^-$ is a weaker reducing agent than $\text{I}^-$, so it cannot give electrons to the weaker oxidiser $\text{I}_2$. This matches the correct statement exactly.

options.A: Correct. Since $\text{Cl}_2$ is a stronger oxidising agent than $\text{Br}_2$, $\text{Br}^-$ can reduce $\text{Cl}_2$ to $\text{Cl}^-$. Since $\text{I}_2$ is a weaker oxidising agent than $\text{Br}_2$, $\text{Br}^-$ cannot reduce $\text{I}_2$. The reaction only goes from stronger oxidiser to weaker oxidiser.
options.B: $\text{Cl}_2$ will oxidise $\text{Br}^-$ and this part is true, but it will also oxidise $\text{I}^-$. Because $\text{Cl}_2$ is above both $\text{Br}_2$ and $\text{I}_2$ in oxidising power, it displaces both. The trap is forgetting that $\text{I}^-$ is an even stronger reducing agent than $\text{Br}^-$.
options.C: Opposite of the truth. $\text{F}_2$ is the strongest oxidising agent of the four, not the weakest. Oxidising power decreases down the group as atoms get larger and attract electrons less strongly, so $\text{I}_2$ is the weakest.
options.D: Opposite of the truth. $\text{I}^-$ is the strongest reducing agent, not the weakest. Reducing power increases down the group as larger ions lose electrons more easily, so $\text{F}^-$ is the weakest reducing agent.
